programs.name: PHAT (Power Hypertrophy Adaptive Training)
programs.author: Layne Norton
programs.summary: A 5-day split with two heavy upper/lower power days (3-5 reps) followed by three bodybuilding-style hypertrophy days that each open with explosive speed sets. Every muscle is trained twice a week, once heavy and once with higher reps and more volume.
programs.evidenceNote: Weekly volume is high (roughly 15-25 hard sets for back and quads, about 12-15 for chest, not counting speed sets), which sits at or above the upper end of what most hypertrophy research supports, so many lifters will need the author's own advice to drop an accessory per day at first. Twice-weekly frequency and stopping 1-2 reps short of failure on most sets match current evidence; the speed work has little direct hypertrophy evidence behind it, and the article gives no numeric load-progression rule.

sources.title: PHAT: Power Hypertrophy Adaptive Training (Biolayne, 2016 repost by the author)

programs.schedule: Day 1 Upper Power, Day 2 Lower Power, Day 3 Rest, Day 4 Back and Shoulders Hypertrophy, Day 5 Lower Hypertrophy, Day 6 Chest and Arms Hypertrophy, Day 7 Rest. Session length is not stated by the author; 90 min is an estimate.

progression.description: Author's current version (Biolayne, posted 2016; same template as the 2011 SimplyShredded original). Power days: 3-5 reps for 3-5 working sets on one main compound each for lower body, pressing and pulling, resting until fully recovered. Speed work: 6x3 at 65-70% of your 3-5RM, explosive, max 90 s rest. Hypertrophy work: 8-20 reps, 1-2 min rest, about 50-75% more volume than the power days. Stop 1-2 reps short of failure on most sets; take only the last 1-2 sets of an exercise to failure, and avoid failure for the first 2-4 weeks while adapting. Rotate power movements every 2-3 weeks. The article gives no numeric weight-increase rule, so incrementKg is null.
progression.deload: Deload as needed (typically every 6-12 weeks) for 1-3 weeks using 60-70% of normal weights. If a lift stalls, target its sticking point with variations (deficit or rack pulls, paused box squats, paused presses).

programs.name: Reddit PPL (A Linear Progression Based PPL Program for Beginners)
programs.author: u/Metallicadpa (r/Fitness)
programs.summary: A 6-day push/pull/legs routine where each day opens with a barbell lift that gets heavier every session, followed by higher-rep bodybuilding accessories. It is meant for beginners and run until linear progression stops working.
programs.evidenceNote: Each muscle is trained twice a week with roughly 10-20 weekly sets for most groups (arms and rear delts get a lot of direct work: 16 sets of curls and 10 of face pulls), which fits current volume evidence; accessories in the 8-12 range taken near failure are well supported. Six sessions a week is a big time commitment for a beginner, and per-session linear progression stalls quickly for lifters who start too heavy.

programs.schedule: 6 days a week as PPLRPPL or PPLPPLR (author prefers Pull, Push, Legs order). The main pull lift alternates deadlift and barbell row, and the main push lift alternates bench and overhead press; both legs days are the same. Optional ab work (weighted planks, ab wheel, hanging leg raises) can be added on squat and deadlift days. Session length is not stated; 75 min is an estimate.

progression.description: Author's original kg figures. Main lifts add weight every session: 2.5 kg for bench, row, overhead press and squat; 5 kg for deadlift (lower is 2.5 kg here because squat is the lower-body lift trained most often). The last set of each main lift is AMRAP with good form. Accessories: when you hit 3 sets of 12 with good form, add weight; if you can't stay in 8-12, lower the weight. Start: work up from the empty bar in sets of 5 until the bar slows, back off 2.5 kg, and start there.
progression.deload: A missed session from poor sleep, food or recovery doesn't count; retry when fresh. If you fail the same session 3 times in a row, take 10% off that lift's working weight and work back up. Move on to an intermediate program when linear progression stalls and recovery between sessions gets harder.

programs.name: PHUL (Power Hypertrophy Upper Lower)
programs.author: Brandon Campbell (Muscle & Strength)
programs.summary: A 4-day upper/lower split with one heavy power day (3-5 reps on the main lifts) and one higher-rep hypertrophy day (8-15 reps) for each half of the body every week. It is built around the basic barbell lifts plus isolation work.
programs.evidenceNote: At 3-4 sets per exercise, chest and back get about 12-16 weekly sets and quads more, trained twice a week with 1 rep in reserve, which fits current hypertrophy evidence. Weak points: the article gives no load-progression or deload rule, hamstrings get comparatively little direct work, and seven 3-4-set exercises often take longer than the stated 45-60 min.

programs.name: Generic Bulking Routine (GBR)
programs.author: Lyle McDonald
programs.summary: A 4-day upper/lower split that trains each muscle twice a week with heavy 6-8 rep sets followed by lighter 10-15 rep sets. It runs in 8-week cycles: two easier ramp-up weeks, then six weeks of adding weight, then you reset and go again.
programs.evidenceNote: About 6-8 sets per muscle per session (12-16 per week), trained twice a week and stopped 1-2 reps short of failure, matches current hypertrophy evidence closely. Direct arm and shoulder work is minimal (1-2 sets of arms per session), exercises are mostly left to the lifter, and the author says it is not for beginners.

programs.schedule: Mon Lower, Tue Upper, Thu Lower, Fri Upper. Sets stop 1-2 reps short of failure (some will reach failure as fatigue builds). Add weight once you reach the top of the rep range (JC Deen's restatement; a reader quotes Lyle as adding weight when the first set reaches the top of the range with a rep or two to spare). No increment is specified.
progression.deload: Built into the cycle: after each 8-week cycle, drop the weights and start over. If the volume is too much, use 2-3x6-8 for the main lifts and 1-2x10-12 for the secondary lifts.

programs.name: Fierce 5 Novice Routine
programs.author: davisj3537 (Bodybuilding.com forum)
programs.summary: A 3-day full-body novice routine alternating two short workouts built on five main exercises each, with the small lifts paired as supersets. Weight goes up every week, and the author says to start lighter than you think.
programs.evidenceNote: Volume is modest (about 5-9 hard sets per muscle per week across A/B), which is enough for true novices and keeps sessions short; the 3x5 compound work has the same hypertrophy potential as higher reps when taken reasonably close to failure. Weak points: little direct chest and hamstring volume, and weekly fixed jumps stall within months, after which the author says to move to an intermediate program.

Archived copy of the original thread (Wayback Machine, July 2024)

programs.schedule: 3 non-consecutive days a week, alternating A and B (e.g. Mon A, Wed B, Fri A, then Mon B, Wed A, Fri B). Author: sessions take just over an hour including stretching and warm-ups.

progression.description: Author's thread as last edited in Jan 2019. Each week add 5 lb (converted to 2.5 kg) to all upper-body lifts and 10 lb (5 kg) to all lower-body lifts. Exceptions: reverse flies +5 lb (2.5 kg) per month, never over 15 lb (about 7 kg) per hand; leg curls (if subbed) +5 lb (2.5 kg) per week; ab work adds a few reps each week. If equipment can't make these jumps, add weight every other week for that exercise and, in the weeks you don't add weight, add 1 rep per set on 5-rep exercises or 2 reps per set on 8-15 rep exercises. Start at 85% of what you think you can lift. Complete first-timers start at 50% and add 10-15% each workout until reaching that 85% level by week 3. While cutting (or for bulking females), use half the increments.
progression.deload: If you fail a lift two sessions in a row, drop that lift 15% (reset) and work back up, focusing on form. A legitimate stall means you still cannot break the plateau after 4-7 days completely off plus a 15% reset. Once you legitimately stall on at least 2 major lifts (bench, rows, squat, deadlift) while bulking, move on; 4-6 months is a typical run.

programs.name: Jacked & Tan 2.0
programs.author: Cody Lefever (GZCL)
programs.summary: A 12-week, 4-day upper/lower program in two 6-week blocks: each day works up to a rep max on a main lift, then does percentage-based volume and high-rep max-rep sets for accessories. The author says its goal is size and work capacity more than peak strength.
programs.evidenceNote: Volume is high and nearly every accessory set is a max-rep set taken to 1-2 reps from failure, which fits current hypertrophy evidence but builds a lot of fatigue, so it suits intermediates with good recovery. Weekly rep-max work on the main lifts is not needed for muscle growth, and the write-up does not say how to set the training max, which you need for the block-1 drop sets.

sources.title: Jacked & Tan 2.0 (Swole at Every Height, Cody Lefever, 4 July 2016)

programs.schedule: 4 sessions a week alternating lower and upper: Day 1 squat-type T1, Day 2 bench or OHP T1, Day 3 the other lower lift (deadlift or squat, different from Day 1), Day 4 the other press. An optional 5th day (an extra T1 variation, or an accessory day with no T1) is not programmed. Back work is mostly T2 and can go on either day type. Session length is not stated; 90 min is an estimate.

progression.description: Author's 2016 write-up (the 2.0 version, which replaces the 2014 original). T1: each session work up to the week's rep max (10/8/6/4/2/1RM in block 1; 6/4/2/5/3/1RM in block 2), then do drop sets. Block 1 drop sets are a percent of a training max (70, 75, 80, 82.5, 85%); block 2 drop sets are 85% then 90% of that day's RM. The last drop set is an optional rep-out. T2a: linear percent-of-TM work (50% x10x4 up to 85% x2x7), recalculated from the week-6 1RM for block 2; the write-up allows 5-10% weekly jumps early and 2.5-5% later. T2b/T2c and T3: find the week's rep max, then 3 max-rep sets with the same weight, 1-2 reps in reserve, 30-60 s rest. The write-up has two conflicting block-2 T2b/T2c lists; this template uses the detailed week-by-week section (15/12/10/6RM, then rest). Its summary table says 12/10/8/6RM. The write-up does not define how to set the TM.
progression.deload: No separate deload. Week 6 has no T2 work, week 11 drops T2b/T2c, and week 12 is only the final 1RM test. If you overshoot a rep max, cut the T1 drop sets by 2.5-5% or one set, or reduce T2 work. If the last-set rep-outs gain nothing for 3+ weeks, use lighter T1 drop sets. If a T2a set can't be completed, lower that lift's intensity.
